groups.title: Components
groups.question: You are building a product page with a reusable card and a page layout that wraps different content. Explain how React components share data and fit together.

followUps.JSX and props: Why shouldn't a child component change its own props?
followUps.Composition and children: How does the children prop help you build a reusable layout component?

evidence.text: JSX is JavaScript syntax that describes what the UI should look like.
Props pass data from parent to child in one direction.
A child treats props as read-only; to change data, the parent owns it and passes down a way to update it.

notEnough: Only saying props are inputs to components.

misconceptions.text: Says JSX is HTML that runs in the browser.

evidence.text: Components are combined by nesting them inside each other.
The children prop holds whatever is placed between a component's tags.
That lets a layout component wrap any content without knowing what it is.

notEnough: Only saying children are the nested elements.

groups.title: Rendering
groups.question: You render a todo list where items can be reordered, and checked items get mixed up after reordering. Explain how React renders and what went wrong.

followUps.Lists and keys: Why does using the array index as a key cause bugs when the list is reordered?
followUps.Render is a pure calculation: Why should a component not fetch data or change variables outside itself while rendering?

evidence.text: Keys let React match each item between renders.
Keys must be stable and unique, such as an id from the data.
With index keys, reordering gives items different keys, so their state ends up on the wrong item.

notEnough: Only saying keys must be unique.

misconceptions.text: Says keys only matter for performance.

evidence.text: A component should return the same UI for the same props and state.
Rendering should not change things outside the component, such as sending requests or editing global variables.
React may render a component more than once, so side effects during render cause bugs.

notEnough: Only saying components should be pure.

groups.title: State
groups.question: A counter shows the old value right after you call the setter, and a form's object state does not update on screen. Explain how React state works.

followUps.useState and re-rendering: Why does logging the state right after calling setCount show the old value?
followUps.Updating objects and arrays: You change one field in a state object directly, and nothing happens on screen. Why?

evidence.text: Calling a state setter schedules a re-render with the new value.
Inside the current render, the state value is a fixed snapshot.
The new value appears in the next render, not in the current one.
Changing the existing object keeps the same reference.
You need to create a new object or array with the change.
React compares references to decide that something changed and re-render.

groups.title: Structure
groups.question: A filter input and a results list are siblings that both need the search text, and you are about to build a new page from a mockup. Explain where state should live and how you would plan the components.

followUps.Lifting state up: Two sibling components need the same value. Where should that state live?
followUps.Thinking in React: How would you go from a mockup to a working React page?

evidence.text: Shared state moves up to the closest common parent.
The parent passes the value and an update function down as props.
State should live as low in the tree as possible so fewer components re-render.

notEnough: Only saying to lift state up.

evidence.text: Break the UI into a tree of components.
Build a static version first that only uses props.
Find the smallest set of state needed and decide which component owns each piece.

notEnough: Only listing the steps without explaining why minimal state matters.
